scenes.title: DynamoDB
scenes.text: During Prime Day, Amazon's own systems call one database more than a hundred million times per second. And most of those calls come back in just a few milliseconds. That database is DynamoDB. Here's how it pulls that off.

scenes.title: What is DynamoDB?
scenes.text: DynamoDB is a database that Amazon Web Services runs for you. You never set up servers, install software, or apply patches. You just create a table and start saving data. It's a NoSQL database, which means it skips the fixed columns and table joins of a traditional SQL database. Instead, it's built around one idea: find any piece of data instantly, using its key.

scenes.title: Tables, items, attributes
scenes.text: Data lives in tables. A table holds items, and each item is a bundle of attributes, a bit like a row in a spreadsheet. But unlike a spreadsheet, items don't need matching columns. One customer might have a phone number. Another might have a list of addresses. DynamoDB only insists on one thing: every item needs a primary key.

scenes.title: The primary key
scenes.text: The primary key has up to two parts. The partition key decides where an item is stored. The sort key is optional, and it orders items that share the same partition key. Picture an Orders table. The partition key is the customer ID, and the sort key is the order date. Now all of one customer's orders sit together, already sorted by date.

scenes.title: Partitions and hashing
scenes.text: So how does it stay fast? Behind the scenes, every table is split into chunks called partitions, spread across many storage servers. When you save an item, DynamoDB runs its partition key through a hash function. That turns the key into a number, and the number points to exactly one partition. To read the item back, DynamoDB does the same math and goes straight to the right place. No searching through the whole table.

scenes.title: How it scales
scenes.text: As your table grows, DynamoDB splits full or busy partitions in two, and spreads them across more servers. Each partition only handles its own slice of the data. So a table with a billion items answers about as fast as one with a thousand. That's the whole trick. The work is divided up, so no single machine ever has to do it all.

scenes.title: Copies for safety
scenes.text: But what if a server dies? Every partition is copied three times, into three separate data centers called availability zones. One copy is the leader. A write counts as saved once two of the three copies have it. If one copy goes down, the other two keep serving traffic, and DynamoDB builds a replacement.

scenes.title: Two kinds of reads
scenes.text: Those copies give you a choice when you read. An eventually consistent read can be answered by any copy. It might be a split second behind, but it costs half as much. A strongly consistent read always goes to the leader, so you're guaranteed the latest data.

scenes.title: Ways to read data
scenes.text: There are three main ways to read. Get Item fetches one item by its full key. That's the fastest. Query grabs items that share one partition key, like all of a customer's orders from March. Scan reads every item in the table. It works, but it's slow and costly on big tables. Need to look things up another way, like by order status? Add a global secondary index. It's a copy of your data, organized by a different key, and DynamoDB keeps it in sync for you.

scenes.title: Watch out: hot partitions
scenes.text: One common mistake is picking a partition key with only a few possible values. If every new item uses today's date as its key, all the traffic lands on one partition while the others sit idle. That's called a hot partition, and it slows everything down. Pick keys with lots of different values, like user IDs, so the load spreads out evenly.

scenes.title: How you pay
scenes.text: You pay in one of two ways. On-demand mode charges for each request, which is great when traffic is unpredictable. Provisioned mode lets you reserve a set number of reads and writes per second, which is cheaper when traffic is steady. Storage is billed separately, by the gigabyte.

scenes.title: When to use it
scenes.text: So when should you use DynamoDB? It shines when you know ahead of time how your app will look up data, and you need speed at any size. Think shopping carts, user profiles, game leaderboards, and login sessions. It's a weaker fit when you need complex joins, or want to ask new questions of your data that you didn't plan for. A relational database or a data warehouse handles those better.

scenes.title: Recap
scenes.text: Quick recap. Tables hold items, and every item has a key. The partition key is hashed to pick a partition. Partitions split as your data grows, and each one is copied three times. Design your keys around how you read, and DynamoDB stays fast, from your first user to your hundred millionth.
